results.result: The authors identified 103 grid cells from 1881 neurons (5.5%) in dorsomedial MEC with field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm using a classification method based on hexagonal symmetry of spatial autocorrelograms compared to shuffled data (99th percentile threshold).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 and C110 provide clear methodological details and quantitative results for grid cell identification. The classification approach using shuffled data controls and statistical thresholds is well-described and appropriate for distinguishing grid cells from other cell types.

results.result: Grid cells exhibited either task-anchored firing (68/103 cells with periodogram peaks at integer multiples of track frequency) or task-independent firing (32/103 cells with peaks at non-integer frequencies), with task-anchored cells showing higher spatial information but similar firing rates. Aperiodic grid cells were rare (3/103) and had lower firing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C38 are well-supported by the Lomb-Scargle periodogram analysis and statistical comparisons shown in Figure 2. The classification scheme is validated by differences in spatial information scores and visual inspection of firing rate maps. The methodological approach using spectral analysis is appropriate for distinguishing these firing modes.

results.result: Grid cells switched between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes within sessions, with 73.8% of cells showing no single mode for >85% of trials. These switches occurred in blocks across multiple trials and could not be explained by trial type or cue availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 are supported by rolling window analysis (Figure 3) and statistical comparison to shuffled data showing non-random block structure (p=0.0003, KS test). The experimental design with interleaved trial types rules out simple explanations based on cue availability. However, the rolling window approach has limited temporal resolution which could affect classification accuracy.

results.result: Grid cells transitioned between firing modes coherently as a population, with strong agreement in firing modes between simultaneously recorded grid cells. Non-grid cells showed more variable behavior, with some switching coherently with grid cells and others maintaining stable task-anchored firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 are supported by agreement score analysis (Figure 4) showing higher coherence between grid cell pairs than grid-non-grid pairs. The findings are consistent with continuous attractor dynamics. However, without recording all grid cells simultaneously, the authors cannot rule out that switching reflects a subset becoming disconnected from the network (acknowledged in C67).

results.result: On cued trials, behavioral performance (stopping behavior and hit rate) was similar regardless of whether grid cells were task-anchored or task-independent, suggesting grid representations are not required for cued reward localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C58, and C78 are supported by behavioral data in Figures 5-6 showing no significant difference in performance on beaconed trials between task-anchored and task-independent conditions. This dissociation between neural state and behavior argues against a general role for grid cells in all spatial tasks.

results.result: On non-beaconed and probe trials (without visual cues), task-anchored grid firing was associated with spatially organized stopping behavior and higher success rates compared to task-independent firing, indicating that grid cell anchoring selectively enhances path integration-dependent performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C59, C87, C6-C7, and C60 are supported by behavioral analyses showing significant differences in stopping organization and hit rates between task-anchored and task-independent conditions on uncued trials (Figures 5-6). Statistical analyses using mixed-effects models support these conclusions. This is the main finding of the paper.

results.result: Grid firing can operate in two distinct modes: anchored to the task environment (providing position information) or independent of the task reference frame (encoding distance traveled). Both modes can be observed during the same behavioral task.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C62, C65, and C66 summarize the core finding that grid cells exhibit dual coding modes. This is well-supported by the periodogram analyses (Figure 2) and within-session switching data (Figures 3-4). The finding extends prior work on circular tracks to a goal-directed task.

results.result: Non-grid cells in MEC form multiple populations: some switch modes coherently with grid cells while others maintain stable task-anchored representations independently. Task-independent periodic activity was rare among non-grid cells, suggesting the MEC implements multiple parallel spatial computations.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C64, C70-C72 are supported by analyses showing differential behavior of non-grid cell populations (Figures 2E, 3-supplement 5, Figure 4). The diversity of non-grid cell responses suggests functional heterogeneity. However, C72 is somewhat speculative about the mechanistic interpretation of multiple sub-networks.

results.result: Grid representations support specific roles in path integration-dependent behaviors but are not required for cued recall of locations, arguing against the idea that grid codes provide a general-purpose spatial representation used across all spatial tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C63, C79-C80, and C88 represent the main conclusion integrating behavioral and neural findings. This is well-supported by the dissociation between cued and uncued trial performance as a function of grid cell state. The conclusion is consistent with prior work on path integration deficits following grid cell manipulations.

results.result: Residual localization performance on task-independent trials suggests additional neural mechanisms may support path integration-dependent behavior, potentially through ramping activity or distance information from task-independent grid representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 acknowledge that some successful performance occurs without task-anchored grid firing. While C90 is supported by the data, C91-C92 are speculative about alternative mechanisms. The manuscript does not provide direct evidence for these alternative mechanisms, making this conclusion uncertain.

results.result: The mode switching observed differs from previously reported spontaneous remapping in that it involves transitions between task-anchored representations (potentially useful for the task) and task-independent representations (unlikely to contribute to task performance).
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 distinguish the current findings from prior work (Low et al., 2021). The distinction is supported by the behavioral correlates showing differential performance. However, C67 acknowledges a limitation that without recording all grid cells simultaneously, the possibility of subset disconnection cannot be ruled out.

results.result: Task-independent coding by grid cells is unlikely to result from failure of upstream visual circuits, as mice performed well on visually cued trials when grid cells were task-independent. Switching may reflect modulatory pathways reducing visual input impact on the grid system.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is a reasonable inference from the behavioral data showing intact cued performance during task-independent firing. However, C77 is speculative about mechanisms (modulatory pathways, top-down control, brain state shifts) without direct evidence. Alternative explanations are not fully ruled out.

results.result: Rather than being an 'always on' tracking system, grid cell networks vary in their engagement with the environment, potentially reflecting attentional/top-down control or indirect consequences of hippocampal place cell map control mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by the variability in grid cell anchoring demonstrated throughout the paper. However, C96-C97 are speculative about underlying mechanisms without direct experimental evidence. These represent hypotheses for future investigation rather than supported conclusions.

results.result: The study used 9 male C57BL/6J mice in a virtual reality location memory task with a 200 cm track containing beaconed, non-beaconed, and probe trials delivered in repeating blocks. Neural data were analyzed using quality metrics (firing rate >0.2 Hz, isolation >0.9, noise overlap <0.05, SNR >1).
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C109 describe the experimental methods and are directly supported by the Materials and Methods section. The experimental design is clearly described with appropriate controls and quality metrics for data analysis.

results.result: Prior work has shown that in circular track environments, grid firing patterns are maintained but no longer anchored to the environment, encoding distance traveled rather than absolute position. Grid representations can also be unstable with spontaneous remapping, but it was unclear whether this impacts spatial task performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 accurately summarize prior work (Jacob et al., 2019; Low et al., 2021) and identify the knowledge gap addressed by the current study. These claims provide appropriate context for the experimental questions.

results.result: Prior MEC manipulation studies show that lesions disrupt hippocampal place representations and impair spatial memory, while NMDA receptor deletion reduces grid cells and impairs path integration. Stellate cell inactivation impairs both path integration and cue-based navigation, but it is difficult to establish whether impairments result from grid firing deficits per se or other circuit alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C19 accurately summarize prior experimental work with appropriate citations. The critical evaluation in C18-C19 correctly identifies limitations of perturbation approaches, providing motivation for the correlational approach used in the current study.

results.result: Prior work shows that inactivation of MEC stellate cells causes deficits in the location memory task and other cued tasks, and that efficient reward localization on uncued trials relies on path integration. Spatial representations for cued tasks could be encoded by other MEC cell types such as border cells, ramping cells, or cue-responsive cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 and C86 accurately cite prior experimental work. Claim C85 is speculative but appropriately framed as a possibility and supported by citations to work on other cell types. These claims provide context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: The results offer a new perspective on interindividual differences in human path integration, suggesting differences could result from variation in grid representation anchoring rather than path integration per se. This could be important for understanding deficits in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are speculative extensions to human cognition and clinical populations. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations to relevant human literature, there is no direct evidence from the current study linking grid cell anchoring variability to individual differences or clinical deficits.

results.result: Grid cells exhibit two distinct firing modes: task-anchored firing (68/103 cells) where activity is anchored to the virtual track reference frame, and task-independent firing (32/103 cells) where periodic activity is decoupled from the task environment and encodes distance traveled independently.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge and accept this core finding. The editor states 'the authors demonstrate that grid cells can either fire in relation to the position relative to task-relevant virtual stimuli or independently based on the distance covered,' and Reviewer 3 confirms 'grid cells could fire in at least two modes' with task-anchored and task-independent characteristics. The data classification and periodogram analysis are not questioned.

results.result: Grid cells can switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes within a single behavioral session, with 73.8% of grid cells showing no single coding scheme accounting for more than 85% of trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'the anchoring of activity patterns could switch within a behavioral session' as a strength of the study. The within-session variability is treated as a key observation that distinguishes this work from prior studies.

results.result: Grid cells transition between firing modes coherently as a population, with simultaneously recorded grid cells switching at the same time, consistent with continuous attractor dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the coherent switching observation. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors found that, interestingly, grid cell activity pattern could be anchored to task reference frame or maintain a periodic pattern independent of the reference frame' and notes the population-level coordination. The interpretation regarding attractor dynamics is not challenged.

results.result: Non-grid cells in MEC form multiple populations: some switch coherently with grid cells while others maintain stable task-anchored representations independently, with task-independent periodic firing being rare among non-grid cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies this as a weakness, noting 'it is unclear whether and how the coding scheme is associated with behavior' for non-grid cells. While the observation of heterogeneity is accepted, reviewers indicate the functional significance and behavioral relevance of these distinct non-grid populations requires further investigation.

results.result: On cued trials where the reward location is marked by a visual beacon, behavioral performance is similar regardless of whether grid cells are task-anchored or task-independent, suggesting grid representations are not required for cued navigation.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'their findings convincingly reveal that mice exhibited better performance in the path integration task when grid cell activity was anchored' and Reviewer 3 notes 'when a unique visual cue marked the reward location, navigation performance was not correlated with the grid cells' firing mode.' This dissociation is accepted as a key finding.

results.result: On non-beaconed and probe trials requiring path integration, task-anchored grid firing is associated with spatially organized stopping behavior and higher success rates compared to task-independent firing.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm this central finding. The editor emphasizes 'mice exhibited better performance in the path integration task when grid cell activity was anchored to their position on the virtual track rather than the distance traversed.' Reviewer 3 states 'on trials in which the rewarded location was unmarked, the behavioral performance of mice was better when grid cells fired in the task-anchored mode.' This correlation is treated as convincing evidence.

results.result: Task-anchoring of grid cells to the environment selectively enhances performance when path integration is required, supporting hypothesized roles for grid cells in path integration while arguing against a general-purpose spatial coding function.
results.evaluation: The editor describes the work as 'highlighting the contribution of grid firing to spatial navigation behavior' and Reviewer 3 states 'the link proposed by Clark and Nolan between task-anchored coding by grid cells and navigational performance is a significant step toward better understanding how grid cell activity might support behavioral behavior.' The selective enhancement interpretation is accepted.

results.result: Switches in grid cell firing mode occur in blocks extending across multiple trials and cannot be explained by variation in cue or reward availability, with block length distribution significantly different from shuffled data.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical question about causality: 'whether the activity anchoring switched first, or the task behaviors altered first, or whether they happened within the same trial' to determine if encoding is causal for behavior. While the block structure is not disputed, the temporal relationship and causal direction remain unclear according to reviewers.

results.result: 103 out of 1881 neurons were identified as grid cells with field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm, located in dorsomedial MEC.
results.evaluation: These basic characterization data are not questioned by any reviewer. The grid cell identification and properties are treated as standard methodological outcomes.

results.result: Residual localization performance on task-independent trials suggests additional neural mechanisms beyond task-anchored grid firing may support path integration-dependent behavior.
results.evaluation: This acknowledgment of incomplete dependence on grid anchoring is implicitly accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 3 notes the study is 'correlative' and that 'selective manipulations of grid cell activity on the virtual task will be needed to evaluate whether the activity of grid cells is causally linked,' which aligns with the authors' recognition of alternative mechanisms.

results.result: The mode switching observed differs from previously reported spontaneous remapping of MEC network states, as it involves switching between task-anchored representations useful for the task and task-independent representations unlikely to contribute to task solution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this distinction from prior work. The characterization of the switching phenomenon as functionally relevant (between useful and non-useful representations) is accepted without objection.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C90-C92. Both evaluations support the acknowledgment that successful performance can occur without task-anchored grid firing and that alternative mechanisms exist. Both note the speculative nature of alternative mechanisms (C91-C92), with OpenEval marking as UNCERTAIN and peer reviewers accepting this as consistent with the correlative nature of the study.

Strong agreement on claims C26-C28 regarding grid cell identification methodology. Both evaluations support these basic characterization claims without question. OpenEval also includes C110 (quantitative results) which peer reviewers do not explicitly address but implicitly accept.

Strong agreement on claims C6, C56-C57, C59-C60, C87 regarding behavioral differences between task-anchored and task-independent conditions on uncued trials. Both evaluations treat this as a central, well-supported finding. OpenEval emphasizes statistical support from mixed-effects models; peer reviewers describe it as 'convincing evidence.'

Agreement on claims C68-C69 distinguishing current findings from prior work (Low et al., 2021). Both evaluations support this distinction. OpenEval also includes C67 (limitation about not recording all grid cells simultaneously), which peer reviewers address separately in R3.

Strong agreement on claims C55, C58, C78 regarding no performance difference on beaconed trials between conditions. Both evaluations support this dissociation as key evidence. Peer review also includes C79 (broader interpretation about selective enhancement), which OpenEval addresses in R9.

Partial agreement on claims C54, C64, C70-C71 regarding non-grid cell heterogeneity. OpenEval supports these observations but notes C72 is speculative. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, specifically questioning the behavioral relevance and functional significance of distinct non-grid populations, indicating this requires further investigation.

Both address the core dual coding finding (C2, C62). OpenEval groups C2, C62, C65-C66 together as the main finding, marking as SUPPORTED. Peer review focuses on C2, C29-C31, C62 and also marks as SUPPORTED, with all reviewers explicitly accepting this classification. Both treat the dual modes as well-established.

Both address periodogram analysis and firing mode classification (C29-C31). OpenEval evaluates C29-C38 as SUPPORTED based on Lomb-Scargle analysis. Peer review includes C29-C31 with C2, C62 as the accepted core finding. Both agree the classification methodology is sound.

Both address coherent switching among grid cells (C47-C48, C53). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED with acknowledgment of limitation (C67). Peer review also supports the coherent switching observation, noting population-level coordination. Both accept the attractor dynamics interpretation without challenge.

Both address within-session switching (C39, C41-C42). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED based on rolling window analysis, noting limited temporal resolution. Peer review accepts the switching observation as a strength but raises UNCERTAIN evaluation regarding temporal causality - whether activity anchoring or behavior changed first. This represents a key difference in interpretation.

Both reference block structure claims (C40, C45). OpenEval supports the non-random block structure (p=0.0003). Peer review marks as UNCERTAIN, specifically questioning the causal direction and temporal relationship between neural switching and behavioral changes. This is a substantive disagreement about interpretation.

Both address the main conclusion about grid cells and path integration (C61, C88). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED, integrating behavioral and neural findings. Peer review also supports this, with reviewers describing it as 'a significant step toward better understanding' grid cell contributions to behavior. Both treat the selective enhancement interpretation positively.

Overlapping coverage of behavioral-neural correlation (C63). OpenEval includes C63 in broader conclusion (C61, C63, C79-C80, C88) marked as SUPPORTED. Peer review includes C63 in the central finding about uncued trial performance (C6, C56-C57, C59-C60, C63, C87) also marked as SUPPORTED. Strong agreement.

OpenEval evaluates claims C76-C77 as UNCERTAIN, noting C76 (intact cued performance during task-independent firing) is reasonable but C77 (speculative mechanisms) lacks direct evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic speculation claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C95-C97 as UNCERTAIN, supporting C95 (variability in grid cell anchoring) but noting C96-C97 are speculative about underlying mechanisms without direct evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these mechanism-focused claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C102-C109 (experimental methods) as SUPPORTED, noting clear description with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers do not provide a separate evaluation of these methodological claims, though methods are implicitly accepted.
OpenEval evaluates claims C22-C25 (prior work summary and knowledge gap) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these literature context claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C12-C19 (prior experimental work and limitations of perturbation approaches) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background literature claims.
OpenEval evaluates claims C83-C86 (citations to prior work and speculation about other cell types) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C99-C101 (extensions to human cognition and clinical populations) as UNCERTAIN, noting reasonable speculation but no direct evidence from current study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these translational speculation claims.

Minimal overlap on claims C49-C51 regarding non-grid cell behavior. OpenEval groups these with C47-C48, C52-C53 about grid cell coherent switching, marking as SUPPORTED. Peer review groups C49-C51 with C4, C54, C64, C70-C71 about non-grid heterogeneity, marking as UNCERTAIN regarding behavioral relevance. Different grouping reflects different analytical focus.
